summary: Round 1, production review of M4.4 (epoch in the commit-chain object path). The mechanism is right and minimal: the epoch is a final field, the key is built in exactly one place, and `git grep 'ctl/log'` over the staged tree finds no second constructor of a chain key anywhere in the eight modules -- so 'every reader and writer updated in the same commit' is satisfied by there being one. Request counts are unchanged and nothing scales with records, shards, partitions or indices: `recover()` still issues one paged LIST of one prefix (R2's recovery exemption), `commit()` still issues one putIfAbsent per attempt plus one GET per lost race, and `logPrefix()` is a String.format, not a store call. The one forward-looking cost consequence -- a reader must learn the current epoch before it can even name the key it wants, so the speculative-GET tail path acquires a lease read it did not have -- is inherent to ADR-0002's design, is already cached per research 03:164, and is owned by M4.5/M4.8; this diff wires no reader, so today's count really is unchanged. Nothing here pre-empts M4.5 (no SEAL/CONTINUE shape, CommitDelta untouched), M4.6 (no seal, no redrive, no lease wired to the commit path) or M4.8 (no ckpt/ segment, no discovery). ON THE ADR QUESTION, since it is the one that decides the shape of this commit: no ADR is required, and I would return that finding if it were filed. The wire-format-change skill's five-contract table does list 'object key grammar', and the bytes do change (`0/` -> `0000000000000000/`), so the skill is on its face in scope -- but every checklist item it carries is either already recorded elsewhere or genuinely vacuous, and I checked each rather than accepting the class. The target grammar including the `:016x` encoding is settled at docs/internal/product/milestones/M4/SPEC.md:129 and again at :269; ADR-0007 binds the slot and the SPEC says in terms that this 'needs no new ADR, because ADR-0007 already binds it'; ADR-0002 and docs/research/30-design-space/03-metadata-and-cas.md:107-115 bind epoch-in-path. A fourth record of a decision written down three times is what the adr skill means by 'an ADR for everything is an ADR for nothing'. Two caveats worth a sentence in the commit body rather than a finding. (a) 'old shape still parses' and 'ship the read side first' are waived here only because no deployment exists and no store in the tree is durable -- that waiver expires the moment M4.6 ships, and the same edit made later would need the epoch-0 prefix readable through a rollout. (b) research 03:110 still writes `<epoch>` unencoded and :164/:240 still write `<podId>`; leaving the corpus alone matches the precedent M4.0 set deliberately when it settled that contradiction in the SPEC, so it is not a defect. ON THE PADDING: the reasoning is sound but its stated basis is forward-dated, and that is worth knowing rather than fixing. Nothing lists across epochs today -- `recover()` lists `logPrefix()`, which is one epoch -- and within an epoch `apply()` folds offsets with `Math::max` and `nextSequence` with `max`, both order-insensitive, so even the SEQUENCE's padding is not load-bearing for the code as it stands. It becomes load-bearing at M4.8's bounded recovery and its zero-LIST discovery, and the SPEC's grammar demands it regardless. Keep it. One thing for the test reviewer, since it sits on the boundary and I did not measure it: `keyFor`'s rendering is asserted by no test, before or after this commit -- the new tests all assert `logPrefix()` -- so by inspection dropping the sequence's `%016x` looks like a surviving mutation, for the max-folding reason just given. ON THE FENCING TESTS: they are not vacuous. `twoEpochsWriteToDisjointPrefixes...` kills a `recover()` that lists the parent `ctl/log/0/` and a `keyFor`/`logPrefix` that ignores the epoch field, and the 9/10/16 test kills `%x` for `%016x` at its second assertion (unpadded, `a` < `10` fails). What they demonstrate is narrower than what they are labelled -- see finding 2. Backlog row: I counted the 17 two-arg call sites myself and the number is right, and the row is honest about the bytes changing rather than burying it. I did not run the suite or clusterTest, so '489 unit tests' and 'clusterTest green' stand as the author's claims under non-negotiable 4, not as anything I verified. The blocking issue is finding 1: the default this commit picks is not a free slot.

findings.title: Epoch 0 is not a leaseless sentinel -- LeaseManager mints it for the first real leadership term, so the default aliases the two
findings.location: sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/CommitLog.java, the 2-arg constructor and its javadoc ("what every call site that has no lease yet still means"), against sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/LeaseManager.java tryAcquire's cold-start path `new Lease(0, podId, endpoint, ...)`, pinned by sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/LeaseManagerTest.java:76 `assertThat(got.epoch()).isZero()`
findings.failure_scenario: The property this task exists to buy is that a writer's epoch names its term, so no two terms share a prefix. That holds for every term except the first. LeaseManager's first acquisition writes epoch 0 -- its own test asserts `isZero()`, and M4.3b's backlog row says so out loud ('two ingesters on a fresh prefix would both have been told they hold epoch 0'). Epoch 0 is therefore simultaneously 'no lease at all' and 'the first leadership term', in the same module, with nothing in the tree recording the collision. Concretely, at M4.6: a fresh cluster's first leader acquires the lease at epoch 0 and, once `new CommitLog(store, prefix, lease.epoch())` is wired, writes to `p/ctl/log/0/0000000000000000/` -- byte-identical to the chain the 2-arg constructor has been writing since M1 and still writes from production `DefaultIngest.java:135`. A pod that has not gone through the lease (the 2-arg constructor stays public and 17 call sites use it) then writes deltas into the LIVE leader's chain, and the leader's `recover()` reads them and assigns offsets from them as though it had committed them. putIfAbsent still gives I1, so nothing is overwritten -- but I3's protection ('readers of the new epoch never look there') is void for that pair, because it is not a different epoch. The javadoc this commit adds states the opposite, so the M4.6 author reads a distinction the code does not have and wires the lease straight in. Every later term (1, 2, ...) is genuinely fenced; the hole is exactly the term the epoch counter starts on, which is also the only term a fresh cluster ever runs in before its first failover.
findings.recommendation: In scope for this commit and cheap: replace the 2-arg constructor's javadoc claim with the true one -- epoch 0 is ALSO the first lease's term (LeaseManagerTest:76), so the leaseless chain and term 0 share a prefix and the fencing property starts at term 1 -- and add the obligation to M4.6's row: either reserve 0 by starting the lease counter at 1, or state why sharing is safe. Do NOT change LeaseManager here; that is the M4.3 family's scope and needs its own red record. If the author's position is that the aliasing is deliberate and harmless, that is a legitimate answer, but it belongs in the tree (staged baselines/review.txt entry or the javadoc), not in a session.

findings.title: The two fencing tests are labelled I3 but demonstrate only its second clause, and the offset assertion pins a state M4.5/M4.6 must change
findings.location: sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/CommitLogTest.java, twoEpochsWriteToDisjointPrefixesAndNeitherSeesTheOthersDeltas (the `THE FENCING PROPERTY ITSELF (I3)` comment and the `sees none of the old epoch's offsets` assertion), and the same claim in the M4.4 backlog row
findings.failure_scenario: I3, verbatim in M4/SPEC.md:101, is 'a reader applies only deltas in a sealed prefix OR a later epoch's chain, never in a discarded suffix'. These tests demonstrate the 'never in a discarded suffix' clause. The 'sealed prefix' clause is not merely untested -- today it cannot hold: `recover()` lists only its own `logPrefix()`, so a CommitLog at epoch 1 starts with every stream's `nextOffset` at 0 and, if anything ever constructed one for real, would REASSIGN offsets epoch 0 already committed, which is I2. The test asserts that state affirmatively ('and sees none of the old epoch's offsets from its own prefix'). Nothing breaks now, because nothing constructs a non-zero epoch. The cost is later: the backlog row records '(I3)' as pinned by a green test, so the next reader concludes the epoch boundary is done and wires lease.epoch() in without M4.5's CONTINUE header or M4.8's checkpoints, which are what carry the offsets across and are the reason the assertion will have to change (the test will still pass -- no CONTINUE object is written in it -- which is what makes the misreading easy rather than loud).
findings.recommendation: Record in the commit body: say in the test comment and in the row that this pins the discarded-suffix half of I3, and that the sealed-prefix/carry-forward half -- without which a new epoch reassigns committed offsets -- is M4.5's CONTINUE plus M4.8's checkpoints, unbuilt.

findings.title: `epoch()` has no caller and no test; `return 0;` is unconstrained by the whole suite
findings.failure_scenario: `git grep '\.epoch()'` over the staged tree returns eight hits, all of them Lease.epoch(); nothing reads CommitLog.epoch(), and the new tests all go through logPrefix() instead. So by inspection the mutation `return 0;` survives -- I did not run it. Harmless today (a getter over a validated final field), but it is public API added ahead of its M4.6 caller, and a reader of the row would reasonably assume the accessor is exercised by the tests the row describes.
findings.recommendation: Record in the commit body: keep it and say it exists for M4.6's wiring, or drop it until the caller lands. Not worth a round.
